10-minute-language-microsprints.title: Use a Short Vocabulary Retrieval Micro-Sprint
10-minute-language-microsprints.subtitle: Retrieve a small set of L2 words, check them, and revisit them later
10-minute-language-microsprints.description: Choose a small set of second-language words or phrases, try to retrieve the meaning or L2 form before revealing the answer, correct errors, and revisit the set in later sessions. Ten minutes is only a convenient container, not an evidence-backed dose.
10-minute-language-microsprints.reason: Narrow the inherited generic language micro-sprint to the claim actually supported by the reviewed adult L2 vocabulary literature: spaced repetition becomes more useful when paired with retrieval practice or semantic elaboration that strengthens form-meaning connections. Remove any implication that ten minutes is optimal or that one vocabulary result generalizes to listening, pronunciation, grammar, or communicative fluency.

lifeOsSource.hack: Pick a small set of L2 words or phrases. Try to retrieve the meaning or L2 form before revealing the answer, check and correct errors, then revisit the set in a later session rather than relying on one massed review.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: Choose a small vocabulary set. For each item, use a cue and try to produce the target meaning or L2 form before looking. Reveal the answer, correct the response, and mark items that need another attempt. Revisit the set in a later session. Use ten minutes only if a short time box helps you start; Brali does not prescribe a universal evidence-backed duration.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: Which items could I retrieve before looking, which errors did I correct, and which items should return in a later session?
lifeOsSource.reference: Rice & Tokowicz (2020) — review of adult second-language vocabulary training

references.title: A Review of Laboratory Studies of Adult Second Language Vocabulary Training
references.claim_scope: Supports spacing plus retrieval practice or semantic elaboration as useful ingredients for adult L2 vocabulary training and form-meaning learning. It does not establish a ten-minute dose, a universal spacing schedule, or equivalent effects for every language skill.

faq.question: Does the session need to be ten minutes?
faq.answer: No. Ten minutes remains only a convenient label and starting container. The reviewed source does not identify a universal optimal session duration. Use enough time to retrieve, check, and correct a small set carefully.

faq.question: Why retrieve before looking at the answer?
faq.answer: The reviewed adult L2 vocabulary literature highlights retrieval practice, especially when combined with spacing, as one way to strengthen learning beyond massed repetition alone. The attempt should still be followed by checking and correction.

faq.question: Does this protocol cover speaking, grammar, pronunciation, and listening too?
faq.answer: No. This reviewed version is intentionally narrow: it is a vocabulary retrieval protocol. Other language skills need practice that matches those outcomes instead of borrowing the vocabulary evidence and stretching it over the whole language.

faq.question: Is one short session enough?
faq.answer: No. The protocol explicitly includes later revisits. The reviewed literature concerns repeated vocabulary training and does not support treating one short exposure as sufficient for durable learning.

intro.html: This protocol uses a short session for one narrow job: retrieving a small set of second-language words or phrases, checking the answers, and returning to them later. A review of adult L2 vocabulary-training studies supports combining repetition with methods such as spacing and retrieval practice that strengthen form-meaning connections. It does not show that ten minutes is an optimal dose or that the same protocol covers every language skill.

sections.title: 1. Choose a small vocabulary set
sections.html: Pick a set small enough that you can attempt retrieval and check each item carefully. Use words or short phrases that matter for what you are learning rather than filling the session with an arbitrary quota.

sections.title: 2. Retrieve before revealing
sections.html: Use a cue such as an L1 meaning, an image, a sentence gap, or the L2 form and try to produce the target before looking at the answer. The point is to make a retrieval attempt, not to stare at the pair again immediately.

sections.title: 3. Check and correct
sections.html: Reveal the answer after the attempt. Correct errors immediately and notice whether the problem was the form, the meaning, or the connection between them. Do not count a confident wrong answer as useful repetition.

sections.title: 4. Revisit in a later session
sections.html: Bring difficult items back later instead of repeating the whole set continuously in one block. Brali does not prescribe one universal spacing schedule here; the evidence supports spacing as a principle, while useful intervals vary across materials and learning conditions.

sections.title: 5. Keep the time box optional
sections.html: If a ten-minute boundary makes the practice easier to start, use it. If the set takes six minutes or fifteen, that is not a failure. The reviewed source supports the learning ingredients, not a stopwatch setting.

sections.title: 6. Practice other language outcomes directly
sections.html: If your real goal is conversation, listening comprehension, pronunciation, grammar use, or writing, add practice that directly requires that skill. Do not assume that better vocabulary retrieval automatically proves improvement in every other language outcome.
